patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Sent abusers away and received them
patterns.role_note: Nunavut → France: Fr Johannes Rivoire; Igloolik (Nunavut) → Belgium: Fr Eric Dejaeger (fugitive 1995–2011); Vancouver → Long Island, New York: Fr Damian Cooper; Canada → Rome: Fr Bernard Prince; Scotland → Toronto: Fr Paul Moore; Newfoundland → British Columbia: Brother Edward English.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Mount Cashel Orphanage: first report 1975, first action 1989 (14 years). Royal Newfoundland Constabulary probe opened Dec 1975 was closed by the police chief nine days later; the Justice Department ordered the report rewritten (1976); Deputy Minister of Justice said further action unwarranted (1977) Graham James (hockey): first report 1996, first action 1997 (1 years). Received a federal pardon in 2007 that became public only in 2010
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases on this map the sources give two dates: the year a complaint first reached the police, a church, an employer or another official body, and the year someone was first charged, convicted or named in an official finding. The middle of those waits is 12 years. In Rochdale in 1968, a pupil told the police about the local politician Cyril Smith and was told that Smith was "a very important, powerful man". In 1970 Smith was assured he would not be prosecuted. In 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged. Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958, and he was never charged while he was alive. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997, and he was first charged in 2016. The map colors each country by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
patterns.role_note: Ontario 2016: Bill 132 (Royal Assent 9 March 2016) removed limitation periods for civil claims based on sexual assault/abuse
patterns.pattern_summary: Most people abused as children do not tell anyone for many years. In many countries and US states the legal deadline for suing or prosecuting, called a statute of limitations, used to run out in a person's early twenties, before most had spoken. When legislatures proposed extending these deadlines or reopening old claims, the institutions that would face lawsuits lobbied against the changes. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million on lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018. In Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Pennsylvania Catholic Conference spent more than $7.6 million and the state's insurance federation nearly $20.7 million on lobbying from 2014 to 2024. These totals cover all the issues they lobbied on, not only this one. Where the deadlines were lifted anyway, many institutions filed for bankruptcy. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and religious orders did so, several of them hours or days before a trial, a deposition or a new law took effect. The Boy Scouts of America and USA Gymnastics also filed.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 1989: Royal Commission of Inquiry into the Response of the Newfoundland Criminal Justice System (Hughes Inquiry), 1989-1992. Officials had transferred offenders and covered up abuse; 11 Christian Brothers convicted; Newfoundland paid C$11.5m compensation in 1996
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. The research for this map found no national inquiry in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Msgr Carlo Alberto Capella, Holy See nunciature in Washington: Convicted by a Vatican tribunal 2018: five years and a €5,000 fine — not tried in the US or Canada
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 1 documented adoption flows into Canada on this map.
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: Vietnam — Operation Babylift (1975): not all children were orphans (receiving or involved). Canada — Sixties Scoop: Ontario ruling 2017 and C$800m settlement. Indian Residential Schools — Truth and Reconciliation Commission and abuse claims. Canada — maternity homes and post-war adoptions of unmarried mothers' babies.
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children from their families were carried out by governments as a matter of policy. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, about 500 babies were taken from mothers held in detention and given to other families; in 2012 a court found this had been a "systematic plan", and by July 2025, 140 of those children had been identified. Under Franco's dictatorship in Spain, children were taken from Republican mothers and later from unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children from their families and placed them in residential schools or with non-Indigenous families. In 1951 Denmark sent a group of Greenlandic children to live with Danish families, and France moved children from the island of Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported children from occupied parts of Ukraine; in March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over these deportations.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 1997: Canada: Criminal Code extraterritorial child sex tourism provisions (Bill C-27 in force 26 May 1997; Bill C-15A 23 July 2002); up to 14 years
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role: Police ran abuse sites to catch users
patterns.role_note: Childs Play — run by Australia's Task Force Argos for 11 months (police ran abuse sites to catch users). Duplessis Orphans (Quebec) — healthy orphans falsely certified mentally ill and confined (claimed, not established).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect networks that abuse children circulate widely. The records gathered for this map show a few cases where a state service was involved, several claims that investigations found to be false, and some that remain unproven. In Chile, Paul Schäfer, who founded the German settlement Colonia Dignidad in 1961, was convicted in 2006 of abusing children there; Chilean officials believe the Pinochet dictatorship used the settlement to torture its opponents, and Germany admitted in 2016 that its embassy had failed to act. In West Berlin, from the late 1960s, the city's youth authorities placed boys in foster care with men known to be paedophiles, on the advice of the psychologist Helmut Kentler. In Afghanistan, US soldiers were told not to intervene when Afghan commanders allied with them abused boys. In Bosnia around 2001, UN police monitors and employees of a US contractor bought women and girls who had been trafficked. In the United States and Australia, police took over websites used to share abuse images and kept them running for weeks or months to identify the users. Investigations found no evidence that MI5 used the Kincora boys' home in Belfast for blackmail, and the ring of powerful men that London police investigated in Operation Midland was invented by Carl Beech, who was later jailed. The claim that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency has not been established.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Banks and firms fined, sued or settled
patterns.role_note: Aylo (Pornhub owner) — DOJ deferred prosecution: Deferred prosecution agreement (21 Dec 2023, Brooklyn) over unlawful monetary transactions involving sex-trafficking proceeds (GirlsDoPorn — adult victims); paid over $1.8m plus victim compensation
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Canada — Sixties Scoop: Ontario ruling 2017 and C$800m settlement; Indian Residential Schools — Truth and Reconciliation Commission and abuse claims; Mount Cashel Orphanage, St John's — Hughes Royal Commission; Nova Scotia Home for Colored Children — Restorative Inquiry; Cornwall Public Inquiry — institutional responses to historical abuse; Grandview Training School for Girls, Galt, Ontario; Ontario training schools class action (Brown v. Ontario); Duplessis Orphans (Quebec) — healthy orphans falsely certified mentally ill and confined; Childs Play — run by Australia's Task Force Argos for 11 months; Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto; Fr Johannes Rivoire — Oblate in Nunavut, never extradited from France; Mount Cashel Orphanage — Hughes Royal Commission; Indian Residential Schools run by Catholic entities — TRC and papal apology; Canada residential schools run by Anglican, United and Pr.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 238 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: British child migration programmes — IICSA
cases.who: UK government; Fairbridge Society, Barnardo's, Sisters of Nazareth, Catholic Church agencies and others; receiving institutions incl. Christian Brothers
cases.what: IICSA's report of 1 March 2018 found that the child migration programmes were 'a deeply flawed government policy' and that successive UK governments failed to ensure protections against abuse. It found a catalogue of evidence that migrated children suffered ill-treatment and abuse including sexual abuse; Barnardo's suspended migration after sexual abuse came to light at its Picton school, and the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to allegations at its schools in Canada and Australia. It recommended an immediate financial redress scheme for surviving child migrants.
cases.cover_up: Successive governments continued the policy despite years of evidence that children were suffering, including sexual abuse. Fairbridge failed to respond properly to a series of sexual abuse allegations at its schools.

cases.title: Mount Cashel Orphanage, St John's — Hughes Royal Commission
cases.who: Mount Cashel Orphanage run by the Irish Christian Brothers, with privileged foster-home status from Newfoundland Social Services; Royal Newfoundland Constabulary; provincial Department of Justice
cases.what: Complaints of abuse at Mount Cashel surfaced in 1974 and 1975 but neither led to charges. Police reopened the case in February 1989; nine Christian Brothers were convicted. The Hughes Royal Commission (156 hearing days, over 200 witnesses, report 31 May 1991) found neither the police nor the Justice Department handled the 1975–76 files normally, and that child welfare director Frank Simms insisted on special treatment for the Brothers. The province paid $11 million to more than 40 victims in 1997.
cases.cover_up: In December 1975 the police chief and assistant chief ordered Detective Robert Hillier to end his investigation after two Brothers admitted molestation; references to sexual assault were removed and the first report destroyed. The Justice Department laid no charges, and four Brothers were moved out of the province instead.

cases.title: Cornwall Public Inquiry — institutional responses to historical abuse
cases.who: Cornwall Community Police Service, Ontario Provincial Police (Project Truth), local probation office, Roman Catholic Diocese of Alexandria-Cornwall
cases.what: The Cornwall Public Inquiry under Commissioner G. Normand Glaude reported in December 2009 at a cost of over $50 million. It found systemic failures by police, probation and the Catholic diocese in responding to historical sexual abuse allegations against adults in positions of trust in Cornwall. On the long-rumoured paedophile 'clan', Glaude made no finding, saying no investigation had provided conclusive evidence.
cases.cover_up: Commissioner Glaude found the Diocese's $32,000 settlement with complainant David Silmser contained an illegal clause, and called Cornwall police's investigation of his complaint 'deeply flawed', though he found no conspiracy between police and diocese.

cases.title: Fr Johannes Rivoire — Oblate in Nunavut, never extradited from France
cases.who: Oblates of Mary Immaculate (OMI Lacombe Canada; Oblates of France)
cases.what: French Oblate Johannes Rivoire worked in the Canadian North from 1959 to 1993. He faced at least three sexual-abuse charges (1998 warrant) concerning Inuit children in Arviat, Rankin Inlet and Naujaat, and a 2022 warrant for indecent assault on a girl in Arviat and Whale Cove between 1974 and 1979. A March 2024 review by retired Quebec justice André Denis, commissioned by the Oblates, concluded on the preponderance of evidence that he assaulted six children. Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami called his death without trial in April 2024 'a systemic failure of nation states and religious institutions'.
cases.cover_up: He left for France in January 1993; a Canadian arrest warrant followed in 1998 and charges were later stayed. A 2022 warrant led to an extradition request that French authorities denied. The 2024 Denis review found the RCMP never contacted the Oblates when charges were laid. In February 2024 the Vatican ruled against his dismissal. He died in France in 2024 without trial.

cases.title: Canada residential schools run by Anglican, United and Presbyterian churches
cases.who: Anglican Church of Canada (ran over 30 schools), United Church, Presbyterian Church, with the Catholic Church and federal government
cases.what: Canada's Indian residential schools were run for the federal government by the Anglican, Catholic, Presbyterian and United churches; the Anglican Church of Canada operated more than 30. In April 2013 Truth and Reconciliation Commission chair Justice Murray Sinclair said about 37,000 former students had filed claims for sexual abuse, serious physical abuse or other wrongful acts, and asked the public to imagine 'a school where half of the students suffered sexual and physical abuse'. The TRC's final report followed in 2015. Under the 2006 Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement, to which the Anglican, Presbyterian and United churches were parties (Anglicans ran about 30% of schools, the United Church about 10%), the Independent Assessment Process for sexual and serious physical abuse had paid C$3.18 billion to 31,103 former students by 31 March 2019 (all churches combined).
cases.cover_up: The schools were a federal government system run by churches.

cases.title: Childs Play — run by Australia's Task Force Argos for 11 months
cases.who: Childs Play (Tor forum; owner Benjamin Faulkner, convicted)
cases.what: Childs Play launched on Tor on 15 April 2016 and, with over a million registered profiles, was described as the largest site of its kind. Its Canadian administrator, Benjamin Faulkner, was arrested in Virginia in early October 2016 with American Patrick Falte; in September 2017 a federal judge in Virginia sentenced both to life for sexually abusing a toddler, and in August 2019 both received 35 years for running a child exploitation enterprise on the related Giftbox Exchange site. Australia's Task Force Argos then ran Childs Play for 11 months, until September 2017, as part of Operation Artemis, to identify victims and offenders.
cases.cover_up: Queensland Police Task Force Argos operated the site for about 11 months (2016–2017), impersonating the owner and posting abuse images to keep users' trust; a UNICEF Norway legal adviser and Amnesty International criticised this, ECPAT supported it, and a York University criminologist called the server move to Australia 'jurisdiction shopping'.

cases.title: Landslide Productions / Operations Avalanche and Ore
cases.who: Landslide Productions (payment portal, Thomas and Janice Reedy)
cases.what: Landslide, a Fort Worth, Texas portal run by Thomas and Janice Reedy, processed credit-card sign-ups for third-party sites, some offering child abuse images. US agents raided it in August 1999; a jury convicted Thomas Reedy, who was sentenced to 1,335 years (reduced to 180 on appeal), and Janice Reedy got 14 years. US Operation Avalanche examined about 35,000 names on the database, and the FBI passed details of 7,272 British residents to UK police, starting Operation Ore, Britain's biggest computer crime investigation; raids began in May 2002. CEOP said 140 children had been rescued in the UK. Later forensic examination showed large-scale credit card fraud in Landslide's records (54,348 sets of stolen card details), and some people were wrongly accused; a legal challenge in 2009 argued that many convictions for incitement rested on flawed credit-card evidence. Follow-on operations took place in other countries.
cases.cover_up: Later reconstruction of the Landslide data found many listed names were victims of credit-card fraud, and the validity of UK Operation Ore procedures was questioned; an estimated 33 suicides followed in the UK.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: China — intercountry adoption programme ended (2024) after trafficking cases
cases.who: China Center for Children's Welfare and Adoption; state orphanages
cases.what: China opened intercountry adoption in 1992; about 160,000 children were sent abroad, peaking at almost 8,000 to the US in 2005. The programme came to depend increasingly on abuse, abduction and trafficking (New Yorker), including Hunan orphanages buying trafficked babies (2005). On 5 September 2024 the foreign ministry announced the end of the programme, except adoption by blood relatives or of a stepchild.

cases.title: Indian Residential Schools — Truth and Reconciliation Commission and abuse claims
cases.who: Government of Canada; schools operated by the Catholic, Anglican, United and Presbyterian churches
cases.what: About 150,000 First Nations, Métis and Inuit children attended federally funded, church-run residential schools; the last closed in 1997. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission's final report (December 2015) documented 3,200 deaths and said the true number is much higher. By the end of 2014, 37,951 claims had been made for injuries from physical and sexual abuse and 30,939 resolved. The Independent Assessment Process received 38,276 claims in total; adjudicators awarded $2.14 billion to 23,431 claimants and the government compensated 4,415 more directly.
cases.cover_up: Under the settlement, claimants' IAP records are to be destroyed after 19 September 2027 unless the claimant asks to keep or share them.

cases.title: Nova Scotia Home for Colored Children — Restorative Inquiry
cases.who: Nova Scotia Home for Colored Children (provincially funded orphanage for Black children)
cases.what: Former residents of the home, which operated from 1921, described neglect and emotional, physical and sexual abuse. A class action was settled and the provincial government apologised in 2014 to former residents and the African Nova Scotian community for harm caused by systemic racism. The Restorative Inquiry delivered its final report on 28 November 2019 in Halifax.

cases.title: Grandview Training School for Girls, Galt, Ontario
cases.who: Ontario provincial training school for girls (juvenile reformatory)
cases.what: Hundreds of women reported physical and sexual abuse while held as girls at the Grandview Training School, a government-run school for 'troubled' girls in Galt (now Cambridge), Ontario, which closed in 1976. Eight former staff members were charged and two were convicted. Earlier sources not re-checked for this map also cite an investigation by Ontario Provincial Police and Waterloo Regional Police after the abuse became public in 1991, a survivors' group of more than 300 women seeking compensation, and a 1999 apology by MPP Jim Flaherty in the Ontario legislature on the province's behalf (these three points not re-confirmed in this pass).
cases.cover_up: Complaints of serious sexual abuse made by girls while at the school were reportedly ignored and never investigated.

cases.title: Duplessis Orphans (Quebec) — healthy orphans falsely certified mentally ill and confined
cases.who: Government of Quebec under Maurice Duplessis; Catholic religious orders running orphanages and hospitals
cases.what: Under Premier Maurice Duplessis, many poor or illegitimate children in Quebec who were not mentally ill were sent in the 1940s and 1950s to church-run psychiatric institutions so that the orphanages could qualify for extra federal aid; Wikipedia, citing historians, gives subsidies of $2.75 a day for psychiatric patients against $1.25 for orphans. Survivors say they were beaten, sexually abused, and subjected to electroshock and lobotomies. Premier Lucien Bouchard apologised in 1999. In July 2001 the orphans accepted Quebec's final offer of $10,000 per person plus $1,000 for each year of wrongful confinement, about $25,000 each, not covering sexual or other abuse; about 3,000 were then still alive. Claims linking the orphans to CIA MKUltra experiments are not established by the sources consulted.
cases.cover_up: No criminal charges resulted from the 1990s complaints; the 2001 compensation excluded victims of sexual or other abuse.

cases.title: Indian Residential Schools run by Catholic entities — TRC and papal apology
cases.who: Catholic dioceses and orders (incl. Oblates of Mary Immaculate) that ran about 44 of 80 schools at the 1931 peak (TRC says about 70% overall)
cases.what: More than 150,000 First Nations, Métis and Inuit children were forced to attend Canada's government-funded residential schools between the 1870s and 1997; the Catholic Church ran over half of them. In 2015 the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's chair said the commissioners had concluded that 'cultural genocide' was the best description of the system. In July 2022 at Maskwacis, Alberta, Pope Francis asked forgiveness 'for the wrong done by so many Christians to the Indigenous peoples', and on his return flight described the system as genocide.
cases.cover_up: Federal government funded and mandated attendance; Catholic entities cited lack of funds to compensate

cases.title: Canada — Sixties Scoop: Ontario ruling 2017 and C$800m settlement
cases.who: Federal government of Canada and provincial child welfare authorities
cases.what: From the 1950s into the 1980s thousands of Indigenous children were taken from their families by child welfare authorities and placed with non-Indigenous foster and adoptive families. On 14 February 2017 Justice Edward Belobaba of the Ontario Superior Court (Brown v. Canada) ruled that Ottawa had failed in its duty of care to on-reserve children in Ontario removed between 1965 and 1984, who lost their language, culture and identity; the class was expected to number about 16,000. On 6 October 2017 Crown-Indigenous Affairs Minister Carolyn Bennett announced an agreement in principle worth about C$800 million: C$750 million for First Nations and Inuit people removed between 1951 and 1991 (C$25,000 each if there were more than 20,000 claimants, up to C$50,000 if fewer) and C$50 million for a reconciliation and healing foundation.

cases.title: Ontario training schools class action (Brown v. Ontario)
cases.who: Government of Ontario provincial training schools (juvenile reformatories)
cases.what: In the class action Brown v. Ontario, the province agreed to a settlement of up to CAD 60 million, signed 21 January 2026 and approved by the Ontario Superior Court on 21 May 2026, for former residents of 13 provincial training schools between 1953 and 1984. It covers physical and sexual assault and solitary confinement. Ontario denies liability and the court did not decide the merits.

flows.title: Seoul → Canada
flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Canada; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.title: UK → Canada child migrants (Home Children)
flows.what: British child migration to Canada began in the 19th century; IICSA found the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to sexual abuse allegations at its schools in Canada.

flows.title: Czech-produced abuse images → buyers in the EU and Canada
flows.what: A Czech photographer and Swedish partner distributed images of about 70 children to customers abroad.

flows.title: Films made in Ukraine/Romania → distributed by Azov Films, Toronto
flows.what: Primary producers were in Crimea (Ukraine), Romania and Germany; the Toronto firm sold to customers in over 50 countries. Start year approximate.

flows.title: Canada → Nepal (aid-worker offender)
flows.what: A Canadian humanitarian working with street children abused boys at his home in Nepal.

flows.title: Nunavut → France: Fr Johannes Rivoire
flows.what: Rivoire left the Arctic for France in January 1993; Canadian warrants (1998, 2022) went unexecuted and France refused extradition. He died in France in 2024.

flows.title: Igloolik (Nunavut) → Belgium: Fr Eric Dejaeger (fugitive 1995–2011)
flows.what: About to be charged in 1995, the Oblate fled to Belgium; Oblate officials acknowledged knowing he was leaving, and he lived 16 years in Oblate houses despite an international warrant until returned in 2011. In 2015 he was sentenced to 19 years for 32 offences against Inuit children in Igloolik (1978–82).

flows.title: Scotland → Toronto: Fr Paul Moore
flows.what: Bishop Maurice Taylor sent Moore, later convicted (2018) of abusing three children and a student priest, to Toronto and to Fort Augustus.

flows.title: Vancouver → Long Island, New York: Fr Damian Cooper
flows.what: After a 1994 abuse admission, the Archdiocese of Vancouver sent Cooper to a Long Island diocese, where he allegedly committed 'problems of a similar nature'.

flows.title: Canada → Rome: Fr Bernard Prince
flows.what: Prince was appointed to Rome in 1991; a 1993 church letter discussed keeping him hidden in the Vatican rather than facing justice in Canada.

networks.name: South Korea's four authorised overseas adoption agencies (Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
networks.what: The four agencies held guardianship over children and sent them abroad under government policy; Holt sent about half (AP). The TRC (March 2025) found agencies met monthly quotas for foreign partners, falsified orphan status and swapped identities, and that the state failed to supervise them. All four were implicated in the petitions (Guardian, 2023).

networks.name: Indian Residential School system (Canada)
networks.what: Federally funded schools run by churches to assimilate First Nations, Métis and Inuit children; about 150,000 attended. Tens of thousands of claims of sexual and serious physical abuse were compensated under the 2007 settlement.

networks.name: British child migration programmes
networks.what: UK government-backed schemes run by Barnardo's, the Fairbridge Society, Catholic agencies and others that sent children to Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Southern Rhodesia; IICSA found sexual abuse and failure to protect.

networks.name: Scouting organisations (national Scout associations)
networks.what: National Scout associations; the Boy Scouts of America faced more than 82,000 sexual abuse claims in its 2020 bankruptcy and had kept internal 'ineligible volunteer' files on suspected abusers.

networks.name: Orphanage trafficking and orphanage tourism (recruitment of children into institutions for donations)
networks.what: A recurring pattern in which orphanages are set up or kept full to attract foreign donations, volunteers and tourists, recruiting children who mostly have living parents, sometimes with payments to families or forged documents. Governments and the US State Department have recognised it as trafficking, and Australia's parliament classed it as modern slavery in 2017.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Ireland → United States: Fr Brendan Smyth.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
patterns.role_note: 2000: Statute of Limitations (Amendment) Act 2000 (passed 21 June 2000) gave a one-year window to bring claims for sexual abuse suffered as a minor and introduced a disability-based extension
patterns.pattern_summary: Most people abused as children do not tell anyone for many years. In many countries and US states the legal deadline for suing or prosecuting, called a statute of limitations, used to run out in a person's early twenties, before most had spoken. When legislatures proposed extending these deadlines or reopening old claims, the institutions that would face lawsuits lobbied against the changes. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million on lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018. In Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Pennsylvania Catholic Conference spent more than $7.6 million and the state's insurance federation nearly $20.7 million on lobbying from 2014 to 2024. These totals cover all the issues they lobbied on, not only this one. Where the deadlines were lifted anyway, many institutions filed for bankruptcy. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and religious orders did so, several of them hours or days before a trial, a deposition or a new law took effect. The Boy Scouts of America and USA Gymnastics also filed.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 1999: Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse (Laffoy, then Ryan Commission), 1999-2009. Ryan Report 20 May 2009: sexual abuse endemic in boys' institutions; religious authorities shielded orders amid a "culture of self-serving secrecy"; state inspectors failed to stop it
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. The research for this map found no national inquiry in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Holy See and the Murphy Commission (Ireland): No Vatican files supplied
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2018: scandal: Tusla refers 126 illegal birth registrations by St Patrick's Guild (May)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role: Welfare state, church and unmarried mothers
patterns.role_note: Ireland — Mother and Baby Homes Commission: 9,000 child deaths; adoptions abroad.
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children from their families were carried out by governments as a matter of policy. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, about 500 babies were taken from mothers held in detention and given to other families; in 2012 a court found this had been a "systematic plan", and by July 2025, 140 of those children had been identified. Under Franco's dictatorship in Spain, children were taken from Republican mothers and later from unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children from their families and placed them in residential schools or with non-Indigenous families. In 1951 Denmark sent a group of Greenlandic children to live with Danish families, and France moved children from the island of Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported children from occupied parts of Ukraine; in March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over these deportations.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 2017: Ireland: Criminal Law (Sexual Offences) Act 2017 gives worldwide jurisdiction over Irish offenders
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Ireland — Mother and Baby Homes Commission: 9,000 child deaths; adoptions abroad; Ryan Commission — state-funded industrial schools and reformatories, Ireland; Mother and Baby Homes Commission — Ireland; Ferns Report — Diocese of Ferns; Murphy Report — Archdiocese of Dublin; Ryan Commission — industrial schools run by religious orders.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 238 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Ferns Report — Diocese of Ferns
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Ferns
cases.what: The state Ferns Inquiry, published 25 October 2005, examined more than 100 allegations of child sexual abuse made between 1962 and 2002 against 21 priests of the diocese. Bishop Donal Herlihy moved accused priests temporarily and then reinstated them, and ordained men he knew or should have known posed a risk. Bishop Brendan Comiskey never got a priest to stand aside from ministry. The report found Garda handling of one of eight formal complaints 'wholly inadequate' and some pre-1988 complaints were not recorded.
cases.cover_up: Bishop Herlihy moved accused priests to other posts or dioceses for a period, then reinstated them; Gardaí failed to record or properly investigate some pre-1988 complaints

cases.title: Murphy Report — Archdiocese of Dublin
cases.who: Catholic Archdiocese of Dublin
cases.what: The Commission of Investigation into the Catholic Archdiocese of Dublin reported on 26 November 2009. It examined a representative sample of 46 priests out of 102 within its remit; 320 people complained of child sexual abuse between 1975 and 2004. It found former Archbishops McQuaid, Ryan, McNamara and Connell failed to report what they knew to the Gardaí, and said the archdiocese's move to take out insurance against abuse claims showed it knew abuse was a potential major cost. It also criticised the Gardaí for treating priests as outside their remit; the Garda Commissioner called the report 'difficult and disturbing reading'.
cases.cover_up: Abuse 'covered up' 1975–2004; bishops generally did not report to Gardaí before 1996; archdiocese took out insurance against abuse litigation from 1987; Gardaí knew of complaints against Fr Tony Walsh in 1990–91 and took no action

cases.title: Ryan Commission — industrial schools run by religious orders
cases.who: Christian Brothers (most boys' institutions), Sisters of Mercy (most girls' institutions) and other Catholic orders
cases.what: The Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse reported on 20 May 2009 after a nine-year investigation of more than 250 church-run institutions that held over 30,000 children from the 1930s to the 1990s. It found sexual abuse 'endemic' in boys' institutions run mainly by the Christian Brothers; the Sisters of Mercy ran most girls' institutions. The 2,600-page report names no perpetrators after a Christian Brothers lawsuit. A parallel state redress scheme paid about 12,000 people an average of €65,000.
cases.cover_up: Christian Brothers sued the commission in 2004 to keep members' names out; no real names of perpetrators published; findings not to be used for prosecutions; state Department of Education inspections failed

cases.title: Landslide Productions / Operations Avalanche and Ore
cases.who: Landslide Productions (payment portal, Thomas and Janice Reedy)
cases.what: Landslide, a Fort Worth, Texas portal run by Thomas and Janice Reedy, processed credit-card sign-ups for third-party sites, some offering child abuse images. US agents raided it in August 1999; a jury convicted Thomas Reedy, who was sentenced to 1,335 years (reduced to 180 on appeal), and Janice Reedy got 14 years. US Operation Avalanche examined about 35,000 names on the database, and the FBI passed details of 7,272 British residents to UK police, starting Operation Ore, Britain's biggest computer crime investigation; raids began in May 2002. CEOP said 140 children had been rescued in the UK. Later forensic examination showed large-scale credit card fraud in Landslide's records (54,348 sets of stolen card details), and some people were wrongly accused; a legal challenge in 2009 argued that many convictions for incitement rested on flawed credit-card evidence. Follow-on operations took place in other countries.
cases.cover_up: Later reconstruction of the Landslide data found many listed names were victims of credit-card fraud, and the validity of UK Operation Ore procedures was questioned; an estimated 33 suicides followed in the UK.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Fr Brendan Smyth — Norbertine order
cases.who: Norbertine order (Kilnacrott Abbey); Fr Brendan Smyth
cases.what: Norbertine priest Brendan Smyth abused children for decades from the 1950s in Northern Ireland, the Republic and the United States; the BBC put the number at at least 143. In 1975 Seán Brady, later Cardinal, attended church meetings where two teenage victims were sworn to secrecy; their evidence was never given to police. The Irish government's delay in acting on the RUC's extradition request led to the collapse of the Reynolds coalition in 1994. He was jailed in Northern Ireland in 1994 for abusing dozens of children there, and in July 1997 was sentenced in Dublin to 12 years for abusing 20 children in the Republic. He died in the Curragh Prison in August 1997. The Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry (2017) found the Norbertine order moved him to another diocese despite knowing his history.
cases.cover_up: Norbertines moved him between parishes, dioceses and countries without reporting him; at a 1975 church inquiry two boys signed oaths of silence; mishandled extradition by the Irish Attorney General's office contributed to the fall of the government in 1994

cases.title: Ireland — Mother and Baby Homes Commission: 9,000 child deaths; adoptions abroad
cases.who: Religious orders (incl. Bon Secours Sisters), local authorities and the Irish state
cases.what: The Commission of Investigation's final report, published on 12 January 2021, covered 14 mother and baby homes and 4 county homes. About 56,000 women and 57,000 children were placed or born in them between 1922 and 1998. About 9,000 children died there, about 15% of all the children in the institutions, with infant mortality about double the national average. The homes doubled as orphanages and adoption agencies, and women faced pressure to place their children for adoption; Ireland did not legislate for adoption until 1952. On 13 January 2021 Taoiseach Micheál Martin apologised for 'the profound generational wrong visited upon Irish mothers and their children'. (The care agent may hold the home-conditions record; this record focuses on removals and adoptions.)
cases.cover_up: In May 2018 Tusla referred 126 cases of births falsely registered by the St Patrick's Guild adoption agency (illegal registrations that hid children's identities).

cases.title: Cloyne Report — Diocese of Cloyne
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Cloyne; Bishop John Magee
cases.what: The Cloyne Report, published 13 July 2011, examined the diocese's handling of allegations against 19 clerics from 1996 to February 2009, after the Irish church had adopted reporting procedures. Nine complaints that should have been reported to the Gardaí were not, and none were reported to the health authorities. Bishop John Magee was found to have shown little interest in applying the guidelines for 12 years. The report said the Vatican's response to the Irish procedures allowed bishops to ignore them.
cases.cover_up: Nine complaints that should have gone to the Gardaí were not reported; none of the 1996–2008 complaints reported to the health service; Vatican's reaction to Irish guidelines described as 'entirely unhelpful'

cases.title: Scoping Inquiry — abuse in religious-run schools
cases.who: 42 religious orders that ran day and boarding schools
cases.what: The state Scoping Inquiry, published 3 September 2024, recorded 2,395 allegations of sexual abuse against 884 alleged abusers at 308 schools run by 42 religious orders, mostly from the 1960s to the 1990s. 590 allegations involving 190 alleged abusers concerned 17 special schools. More than half of the alleged abusers are dead. The government announced a full Commission of Investigation.

cases.title: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
cases.who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
cases.what: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; it held over 250,000 unique videos and its server had more than one million Bitcoin addresses, one per account. IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.
cases.cover_up: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.

cases.title: Freedom Hosting — Tor host for Lolita City and other abuse sites
cases.who: Freedom Hosting (Eric Eoin Marques, convicted)
cases.what: Freedom Hosting was a free anonymous dark web hosting service that ran from July 2008 to July 2013 and hosted over 200 child exploitation websites, including Lolita City, which Anonymous had attacked in 2011. The operator, Eric Eoin Marques, was arrested in Dublin in early August 2013 on a US warrant; the FBI accused him of being 'the largest facilitator of child porn on the planet'. After Ireland's Supreme Court dismissed his challenge in March 2019 he was extradited, pleaded guilty on 6 February 2020 to conspiracy to advertise child sexual abuse material, and on 16 September 2021 was sentenced to 27 years. DOJ said the sites held millions of images and videos, over 1.97 million not previously known to law enforcement.
cases.cover_up: Extradition from Ireland took from 2013 to 2019 through appeals.

cases.title: Diocese of Raphoe — Fr Eugene Greene
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Raphoe
cases.what: Fr Eugene Greene, the most notorious offender in the Diocese of Raphoe, was sentenced in 1999 to 12 years in prison for abusing 26 boys over 20 years. A church safeguarding review published on 30 November 2011 found allegations against 14 Raphoe priests between 1975 and 2010, four of whom had been convicted, and pointed to 'significant errors of judgement' by successive bishops. Former bishop Séamus Hegarty said his past practice was 'sometimes poor' and apologised.

cases.title: Diocese of Stockton — Fr Oliver O'Grady
cases.who: Diocese of Stockton; Bishop Roger Mahony (later Cardinal Archbishop of Los Angeles)
cases.what: Irish-born priest Oliver O'Grady, ordained in 1971 for the Diocese of Stockton, abused children from about 1973 and was moved between parishes. Bishop Roger Mahony knew of concerns by 1980 and moved him in 1984. O'Grady was convicted in 1993 and sentenced to 14 years; a 1998 civil jury awarded $30 million (reduced to $7 million). Paroled and deported to Ireland in 2000, he was convicted there for child abuse images in 2012 and 2020.
cases.cover_up: After police declined to charge him in 1984, Bishop Mahony moved him to another parish and later made him pastor; Mahony said he was unaware of molestation reports, although a letter about earlier abuse was in O'Grady's personnel file.

cases.title: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
cases.who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
cases.what: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

cases.title: Scouting Ireland — 'Historical Sexual Abuse in Scouting: A Learning Review' (Elliott)
cases.who: Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland (CBSI) and Scout Association of Ireland (SAI), merged as Scouting Ireland in 2004
cases.what: Child-protection consultant Ian Elliott's 'Historical Sexual Abuse in Scouting: A Learning Review', published by Scouting Ireland on 14 May 2020, found a cover-up and failure to report abuse in the former Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland and Scout Association of Ireland. It described 'a culture driven by self-interest', said 'cronyism thrived', and found that people suspected or known to be sex offenders gained positions of power and became 'largely impregnable'; records had been lost or destroyed, so the full extent could not be determined. An earlier audit reported to the Oireachtas in November 2018 had found evidence of 108 alleged victims and 71 alleged abusers, with numbers expected to rise considerably.
cases.cover_up: The review found 'coverup and a failure to report abuse'; records were lost or destroyed; adults with a sexual interest in young people rose to positions of influence and prevented known offenders being removed.

cases.title: Marcial Maciel and the Legion of Christ — 2019 internal report
cases.who: Legion of Christ (Legionaries); founder Marcial Maciel
cases.what: For decades until 2006 the Vatican dismissed accusations by seminarians that founder Marcial Maciel had abused them. In 2006 it ordered him to retire to a life of 'prayer and penitence', and on 1 May 2010, after an apostolic visitation, it said his acts were 'true crimes'. The Legion's own report, released on 21 December 2019, found that 175 minors were abused by 33 of its priests between 1941 and 2019; at least 60 of them by Maciel. It said 111 of the 175 were victims of Maciel or of his victims, and that 14 of the 33 abusive priests had themselves been abused within the order.
cases.cover_up: Letters to the Vatican in 1976, 1978 and 1989 and formal charges in 1998 produced no action; Vatican in 2010 said the Legion had shielded Maciel; Maciel never laicised or tried

flows.title: Ireland → United States: Fr Brendan Smyth
flows.what: The Norbertine order knew of Smyth's abuse and moved him between parishes, dioceses and countries, including assignments in the US, sometimes without warning bishops; he abused at least 143 children.

Its North American province filed for bankruptcy in 2011 and paid US$16.5 million to 400 victims.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–).
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children from their families were carried out by governments as a matter of policy. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, about 500 babies were taken from mothers held in detention and given to other families; in 2012 a court found this had been a "systematic plan", and by July 2025, 140 of those children had been identified. Under Franco's dictatorship in Spain, children were taken from Republican mothers and later from unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children from their families and placed them in residential schools or with non-Indigenous families. In 1951 Denmark sent a group of Greenlandic children to live with Danish families, and France moved children from the island of Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported children from occupied parts of Ukraine; in March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over these deportations.

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role: Proven link to a state service
patterns.role_note: Colonia Dignidad (Chile) — child sexual abuse by Paul Schäfer; DINA detention and torture site (proven link to a state service). Colonia Dignidad — Paul Schäfer convicted of abusing 25 children (proven link to a state service).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect networks that abuse children circulate widely. The records gathered for this map show a few cases where a state service was involved, several claims that investigations found to be false, and some that remain unproven. In Chile, Paul Schäfer, who founded the German settlement Colonia Dignidad in 1961, was convicted in 2006 of abusing children there; Chilean officials believe the Pinochet dictatorship used the settlement to torture its opponents, and Germany admitted in 2016 that its embassy had failed to act. In West Berlin, from the late 1960s, the city's youth authorities placed boys in foster care with men known to be paedophiles, on the advice of the psychologist Helmut Kentler. In Afghanistan, US soldiers were told not to intervene when Afghan commanders allied with them abused boys. In Bosnia around 2001, UN police monitors and employees of a US contractor bought women and girls who had been trafficked. In the United States and Australia, police took over websites used to share abuse images and kept them running for weeks or months to identify the users. Investigations found no evidence that MI5 used the Kincora boys' home in Belfast for blackmail, and the ring of powerful men that London police investigated in Operation Midland was invented by Carl Beech, who was later jailed. The claim that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency has not been established.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–); SENAME — deaths and abuse in Chilean state child protection; Chile — 'Informe Jeldres' (Judiciary/UNICEF audit of residential care homes); Colonia Dignidad (Chile) — child sexual abuse by Paul Schäfer; DINA detention and torture site; Colonia Dignidad — Paul Schäfer convicted of abusing 25 children.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 238 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–)
cases.who: Chilean state agencies, hospital and social-service staff, intermediaries
cases.what: Children were taken from mainly poor mothers, some told their babies had died, and sent for adoption to families in the United States and Europe, including Sweden; the practice peaked under the Pinochet dictatorship (1973–1990). A Chilean judge opened a criminal investigation in 2018 covering about 8,000 adoptions abroad from 1970 to 1999. A congressional committee concluded the state was responsible; as of September 2023 nobody had been brought to justice. Sweden opened its own investigation into intercountry adoptions after activism by Chilean adoptees.

cases.title: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
cases.who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
cases.what: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.

cases.title: SENAME — deaths and abuse in Chilean state child protection
cases.who: Servicio Nacional de Menores (SENAME), Ministry of Justice, and accredited private residences
cases.what: The death of an 11-year-old girl at SENAME's Galvarino centre in Santiago in April 2016 exposed conditions in the system; in October 2016 SENAME disclosed 1,313 deaths of people in its programmes between 2005 and mid-2016. In a report released on 30 July 2018 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child found the Chilean state responsible for 'grave violations' of the Convention, including sexual abuse, torture and cruel treatment in SENAME residences over 40 years, overcrowding of up to 60% and 210 deaths in residences 2005–2016. A former national director was questioned as a suspect over children's deaths in 2018.

cases.title: Chile — 'Informe Jeldres' (Judiciary/UNICEF audit of residential care homes)
cases.who: SENAME-accredited residential care homes (hogares), run by private organisations under state supervision
cases.what: Family-court judges led by Judge Mónica Jeldres, with UNICEF, interviewed children in residential homes between July and November 2012. The report found sexual abuse was a constant in the homes and that 10% of children in state protection had been involved in some form of sexual abuse as victim or perpetrator. In one Arica home it found a sexual exploitation network organised by carers: 24 girls left the home and returned drugged at dawn. After publication the government ordered 34 homes intervened, SENAME closed four residences, the prosecutor's office opened investigations and deputies announced a congressional investigating commission.
cases.cover_up: The report was delivered to the Judiciary in March 2013 but held back over methodological criticism until CIPER published it in July 2013; legislators said the Justice Minister had known since March.

cases.title: Colonia Dignidad (Chile) — child sexual abuse by Paul Schäfer; DINA detention and torture site
cases.who: Colonia Dignidad sect led by Paul Schäfer; Chile's secret police DINA; West German embassy
cases.what: Paul Schäfer, a former Nazi army corporal wanted in Germany on child abuse charges, founded the Colonia Dignidad commune in southern Chile in 1961. Chilean officials believe the colony was used as a centre for torture of opponents of the Pinochet dictatorship between 1973 and 1990, and Schäfer was charged with aiding the regime. The colony recruited children from local farms into its free school and clinic; an investigation opened only after Chilean mothers complained in 1997. Schäfer fled to Argentina, was arrested there in March 2005 and returned to Chile, and on 24–25 May 2006 a Chilean court sentenced him to 20 years for sexually abusing 25 children; with further convictions for torture, weapons and a murder his sentences totalled 33 years. He died in prison in 2010. The colony's doctor, Hartmut Hopp, was convicted in Chile in 2011 of 16 counts of aiding child sexual abuse.
cases.cover_up: In 1966 a teenager who fled took refuge at the West German embassy; the embassy sent a delegation and said it found no evidence. German diplomats praised it as a 'model colony'. Federal President Gauck said in July 2016 that German diplomats had for years looked away; Foreign Minister Steinmeier in April 2016 shortened the closure period of Foreign Office files from 30 to 20 years to release them. Schäfer fled in 1997 and was caught in Argentina in March 2005.

cases.title: Germany acknowledges failures over Colonia Dignidad
cases.who: German Foreign Office; Colonia Dignidad
cases.what: In April 2016 Germany released Foreign Office files from 1986–1996 and the foreign minister admitted diplomats had failed colony residents, including abused children. In 2017 the Bundestag formally acknowledged German responsibility and asked the government to plan an investigation, memorial and help for victims; in 2019 Germany announced compensation payments to victims.
cases.cover_up: Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier said in April 2016 that 'over the course of many years, from the 60s to the 80s, German diplomats at best looked away' and that the embassy failed to shield Germans at the colony.

cases.title: Fernando Karadima, Bishop Barros and Chile's bishops' resignation offer
cases.who: Archdiocese of Santiago; Fr Fernando Karadima; Bishop Juan Barros; Cardinals Errázuriz and Ezzati
cases.what: The Vatican found Fr Fernando Karadima guilty of sexual abuse in 2011 and sentenced him to a life of prayer and penance; Pope Francis dismissed him from the priesthood on 27 September 2018, announced the next day. Four of his protégés became bishops, including Juan Barros of Osorno, whom Francis had defended. After receiving a 2,300-page report from Archbishop Charles Scicluna, Francis wrote in April 2018 that he had been mistaken in his assessment of the situation in Chile. Every bishop in Chile offered to resign in May 2018; by the end of June five resignations, including Barros's (11 June), had been accepted. In October 2018 an appeals court found the Archdiocese of Santiago liable for covering up for Karadima in a suit by three survivors naming Cardinals Errázuriz and Ezzati.
cases.cover_up: Parishioners reported Karadima to Archbishop Fresno in 1984; Cardinal Errázuriz shelved a credible 2004–05 investigation; Barros, a Karadima protégé, made bishop of Osorno in 2015

cases.title: Spiniak case, Chile — child exploitation ring and false accusation against a senator
cases.who: Claudio Spiniak (businessman)
cases.what: Businessman Claudio Spiniak was arrested in 2003 accused of leading a network that sexually abused and exploited adolescents. In 2008 Chile's Supreme Court sentenced him to 12 years for sexual abuse of minors, promoting their exploitation and producing pornographic material; he was released in 2013 and died in March 2026. A witness claimed that members of Congress attended his parties — claims publicly backed by a deputy and a former priest — but she later admitted she had lied; the politicians named were cleared (proceedings dismissed for lack of evidence). The political-network claim is disproved.

cases.title: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
cases.who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
cases.what: An international online ring that ran for about four years over encrypted internet chat; each new member had to supply 10,000 images of child abuse. Members held at least 750,000 images and 1,800 videos. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, police in 12 to 13 countries (reported figures differ) acted simultaneously on 2 September 1998, about 1,500 officers raiding 107 homes and making 104 arrests. CNN reported in February 2001 that only 17 of the children in the images had been identified, six of them in Britain. The investigation began after US Customs exposed a related ring, the Orchid Club, in 1996.

cases.title: Marist Brothers Chile — Brother Abel Pérez
cases.who: Marist Brothers in Chile
cases.what: In 2017 the Chilean Marist Brothers acknowledged that Brother Abel Pérez abused at least 14 minors between the 1970s and 2000. He had confessed to superiors in 2010 and was then transferred to Peru. Police investigated complaints at many of the order's schools.
cases.cover_up: After confessing to superiors in 2010, Pérez was transferred to Peru

cases.title: Pope Francis' letter to Chile's bishops and the Scicluna mission (2018)
cases.who: Pope Francis; Archbishop Charles Scicluna; Mgr Jordi Bertomeu
cases.what: After defending Bishop Juan Barros in January 2018, Pope Francis sent Archbishop Charles Scicluna and Mgr Jordi Bertomeu, who took 64 depositions in New York and Santiago; their report ran to more than 2,300 pages. In a letter of 8 April 2018 Francis wrote that he had 'made serious errors in the assessment and perception of the situation, in particular through the lack of reliable and balanced information', and summoned the Chilean bishops to Rome, where all of them offered to resign in May 2018.

flows.what: Children taken from Chilean mothers and adopted in Sweden, peaking under Pinochet; Sweden opened its own inquiry.
