flows.what: After he admitted abusing pupils at St. Blasien (1982–84) and Canisius-Kolleg, the Jesuits said his superiors helped him emigrate to South America, where he lived as of 2010. A separate summary says he had also offended in Jesuit schools in Chile and Spain; his exact destination country is not confirmed.

flows.title: Siegburg, Germany → Chile (Paul Schäfer flees abuse warrant)
flows.what: After Siegburg authorities issued a warrant in 1959 for abusing two boys, Schäfer fled and in January 1961 settled in Chile with a small group of followers, founding Colonia Dignidad.

flows.title: Chile → Argentina (Schäfer in hiding 1997–2005)
flows.what: Charged with child abuse in Chile, Schäfer disappeared on 20 May 1997 and hid in Argentina until found in a gated community in Tortuguitas in March 2005 and returned to Chile.

flows.title: Chile → Germany (Colonia Dignidad doctor Hartmut Hopp flees)
flows.what: Colony doctor Hartmut Hopp, under house arrest awaiting trial, fled Chile for Germany in May 2011. German prosecutors sought in 2016 to enforce a five-year sentence imposed in Chile, then dropped their own investigation in May 2019.

networks.name: Colonia Dignidad / Villa Baviera
networks.what: German sect enclave in Chile led by Paul Schäfer, convicted in 2006 of abusing 25 minors. Used by Pinochet's secret police DINA as a detention and torture site (Rettig Commission 1991). Germany's president acknowledged diplomatic failures in 2016.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

networks.name: Marist Brothers
networks.what: Teaching order founded in France. Listed 154 members accused in Australia (1980–2015); nine Brothers convicted in New Zealand; apologised for systemic abuse at Scottish schools; acknowledged at least 14 victims of one Brother in Chile; complaints against 12 teachers at Barcelona schools.

networks.name: Society of Jesus (Jesuits)
networks.what: The 2010 Canisius-Kolleg disclosures in Berlin started Germany's abuse reckoning. In 2023 El País published the diary of Spanish Jesuit Alfonso Pedrajas recording abuse of more than 80 minors in Bolivia, with superiors aware from 1978.

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Apollo Quiboloy (Kingdom of Jesus Christ): first report 2021, first action 2024 (3 years). Indicted in the US (Central District of California) on 11 Nov 2021 for sex trafficking etc.; refused to cooperate with Philippine inquiries; close ties to President Rodrigo Duterte; Senate arrest warrant March 2024
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases on this map the sources give two dates: the year a complaint first reached the police, a church, an employer or another official body, and the year someone was first charged, convicted or named in an official finding. The middle of those waits is 12 years. In Rochdale in 1968, a pupil told the police about the local politician Cyril Smith and was told that Smith was "a very important, powerful man". In 1970 Smith was assured he would not be prosecuted. In 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged. Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958, and he was never charged while he was alive. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997, and he was first charged in 2016. The map colors each country by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: No national inquiry found. Bishops apologised 9 July 2002; said about 200 of 7,000 priests had sexual misconduct over two decades; at least 34 priests suspended in 2003
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. The research for this map found no national inquiry in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 7,853 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman).
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role_note: 1992: Manila mayor Alfredo Lim closed the Ermita sex-industry district (from 1992); many businesses moved to Angeles City, finding a new customer base among sex tourists, after Clark Air Base closed in 1992 2014: IJM/NCMEC data: Philippine IP addresses used for child sexual exploitation grew more than 12-fold per month from 2014 to 2017; Philippine anti-trafficking unit cases rose from 1 (2014) to 43 (2017); 64% initiated by foreign police referrals 2016: IJM: prevalence of establishment-based child sex trafficking fell 79%-86% in target Philippine cities 2006-2016 — while online exploitation rose 2020: Europol IOCTA 2020: "Livestreaming is becoming mainstream"; the Philippines remains the main country for LDCA, cases surged in lockdown; a large Romanian operation showed it is not limited to Southeast Asia 2022: IJM (2023, Scale of Harm): 1 in every 100 children in the Philippines was a victim of online sexual exploitation in 2022; IJM UK says the UK is among the top three consumer countries
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Where children are abused for paying viewers
patterns.role_note: Australia → Philippines payments for livestreamed abuse.
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No national inquiry into institutional abuse found
patterns.role_note: Bishops apologised 9 July 2002; said about 200 of 7,000 priests had sexual misconduct over two decades; at least 34 priests suspended in 2003
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Philippines — foreign offenders and child sex trafficking in tourist towns (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Foreign offenders; family members; brothel and bar operators
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says sex trafficking frequently occurs in tourist destinations such as Boracay, Angeles City, Olongapo, Puerto Galera and Surigao. Many foreign offenders are convicted or charged sex offenders at home, most commonly from Australia, Japan, New Zealand, the UK and the US, with more reports from Canada, Morocco, Iraq and Denmark. Courts convicted 143 traffickers, 120 for sex trafficking.
cases.cover_up: Corruption and official complicity remained significant concerns.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Peter Scully — pay-per-view abuse streamed from Mindanao
cases.who: 'No Limits Fun' dark web site (Peter Scully, Australian; Filipino accomplices)
cases.what: An Australian from Melbourne who moved to Cagayan de Oro, Mindanao, in 2011 was alleged to have run a ring that abused children and sold videos of the abuse online to customers abroad. The Philippine investigation began with a tip from Dutch police, who found images on a seized hard drive. Arrested in 2015, he was charged with the murder of a 12-year-old girl as well as trafficking and child abuse. In June 2018 a Cagayan de Oro court sentenced him to life imprisonment after convicting him of one count of human trafficking and five counts of rape. On 3 November 2022, under a plea bargain, he was sentenced to a further 129 years; his former girlfriend, a co-accused, got 126 years and two others more than nine years each.

cases.title: David Timothy Deakin — life sentence, Angeles City court (2020)
cases.who: David Timothy Deakin (US national)
cases.what: Acting on an FBI referral, the Philippine National Bureau of Investigation arrested US national David Timothy Deakin in Mabalacat, Pampanga, in 2017, rescuing two girls and seizing hard drives of abuse material; IJM said he abused Filipino children, recorded it and sold it online to foreign customers. In May 2020 the Angeles City Regional Trial Court Branch 58 convicted him of large-scale human trafficking and sentenced him to life imprisonment, in the country's first conviction delivered by videoconference. The 2025 US TIP report names Angeles City among tourist destinations with high demand for commercial sex.

cases.title: Philippines blacklists Australian sex offender after AFP warning (2013)
cases.who: Philippine Bureau of Immigration; Australian Federal Police
cases.what: In April 2013 Philippine immigration officers at Manila airport intercepted and blacklisted an Australian convicted in Perth in 2010 of indecent assault on children, travelling on a New Zealand passport and planning to stay in Iloilo, after an Australian police warning that he posed a risk to Filipino children. It is an example of offender travel notifications between countries.

cases.title: AUSTRAC v Westpac — payments linked to child exploitation in the Philippines
cases.who: Westpac Banking Corporation (failure to monitor transfers)
cases.what: In November 2019 AUSTRAC alleged Westpac had breached anti-money-laundering law more than 23 million times, including failing to report international funds transfer instructions worth more than A$11 billion; the breaches included failures over suspicious transactions associated with possible child exploitation. The scandal forced the resignation of chief executive Brian Hartzer. On 24 September 2020 Westpac and AUSTRAC agreed a record A$1.3 billion penalty, the largest in Australian corporate history.
cases.network: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)

cases.title: Apollo Quiboloy — Kingdom of Jesus Christ
cases.who: Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC)
cases.what: A federal grand jury in the Central District of California returned a 42-count superseding indictment on 10 November 2021 (unsealed 18 November) charging Quiboloy and eight church administrators, including with sex trafficking of children. It alleges females aged about 12 to 25 were recruited as personal assistants and required to have sex with him, and that church members were brought to the US on fraudulently obtained visas and forced to solicit donations for a sham charity. In 2024 the Philippine Department of Justice charged him with sexual abuse and a court ordered his arrest; after a two-week police operation at the church's Davao City compound he surrendered and was taken into custody on 8 September 2024. He denies the charges.

cases.title: Gabriel Matzneff — writer's published accounts of abusing minors
cases.who: Gabriel Matzneff (author); French literary establishment (Gallimard and others)
cases.what: From the 1960s Matzneff wrote openly about sex with adolescents and was feted by the Paris literary world. In the memoir 'Le Consentement' (published January 2020) its author, a publishing executive, described their relationship when she was 14. Paris prosecutors opened an investigation for rape of a minor in January 2020, and Gallimard withdrew his journals from sale. The BBC noted that, given the time elapsed, the case was unlikely to lead to charges. In November 2023 prosecutors opened a second investigation after another woman accused him of raping her as a child. He has not been convicted.
cases.cover_up: Literary tolerance: Matzneff published diaries describing sex with minors and child sex tourism in the Philippines (e.g. 1985) and was celebrated on TV (Apostrophes, 1990).

cases.title: Scale of Harm — prevalence of livestreamed abuse in the Philippines (IJM / Rights Lab)
cases.who: Family members and neighbours paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse
cases.what: IJM and the University of Nottingham Rights Lab estimated the prevalence of trafficking to produce child sexual exploitation material in the Philippines. IJM states that 1 in every 100 Filipino children was a victim of online sexual exploitation in 2022, that the median victim age in its earlier 2020 study was 11, average abuse lasted two years, and 9% of victims were 3 or younger. IJM UK says the UK is among the top three consumer countries.
cases.network: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)

cases.title: Europol sprint on buyers of live-distant abuse in the Philippines (2024)
cases.who: Buyers worldwide directing livestreamed abuse by traffickers in the Philippines
cases.what: From 24 to 28 June 2024, 32 investigators at Europol processed leads from US HSI investigations into networks exploiting children in the Philippines: over 10 million lines of chat between about 12,000 customer accounts and 100 seller accounts, built up over 12 years. The sprint produced information packages that may lead authorities in 24 countries to 197 buyers. Europol notes buyers direct traffickers to abuse children in real time on webcam and some travel to the Philippines to abuse children in person.
cases.network: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them

patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. cases.title: MINUSTAH Sri Lankan contingent — child sexual exploitation ring, Haiti
cases.who: Sri Lanka Army contingent of the UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti (MINUSTAH)
cases.what: In November 2007, 114 members of the 950-strong Sri Lankan contingent were accused of sexual misconduct and abuse, and 108, including three officers, were sent home. cases.cover_up: Repatriation instead of prosecution: 114 Sri Lankan peacekeepers were sent home; Sri Lankan authorities judged the acts 'consensual' and nobody was jailed.

cases.title: Haiti — restavek child domestic servitude and gang exploitation of children (US TIP 2025)

cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says a large share of Haiti's trafficking cases involve children in restavek domestic servitude, often physically abused and unpaid, and that displacement from Port-au-Prince increased children's risk of sexual exploitation in the restavek system. cases.cover_up: Observers report police and immigration officials complicit at the Haiti–Dominican Republic border.

cases.title: Haitian Football Federation — Yves Jean-Bart banned by FIFA

cases.what: On 30 April 2020 The Guardian reported accusations that Jean-Bart, president of the Haitian Football Federation since 2000, coerced young female players at the national training centre in Croix-des-Bouquets into sex; he denies the allegations. On 18 Nov 2020 FIFA's Ethics Committee banned him from football for life. On 14 Feb 2023 the Court of Arbitration for Sport annulled the ban; FIFA appealed to the Swiss Federal Tribunal in March 2023 (outcome not checked). Human Rights Watch said witnesses and survivors had faced threats and intimidation. He has not been convicted by any court.

cases.what: The US State Department's 2019 Trafficking in Persons Report states that Haiti's social welfare agency IBESR, 'after completing an assessment of more than 750 orphanages with another government and international NGOs, identified 3,019 potential victims of trafficking in those institutions'. cases.title: Oxfam GB in Haiti — 2011 investigation; possible involvement of minors not pursued

cases.what: Oxfam GB's 2011 internal investigation found staff in Haiti had used prostitutes, some of whom were alleged to be 'underage'. cases.cover_up: Staff including the Belgian country director were allowed to resign; Oxfam did not report the allegations of abuse of minors to the Charity Commission or police in 2011.

cases.what: The UN verified sexual violence against 566 children (523 girls, 43 boys) in Haiti in 2024, 411 attributed to the Viv Ansanm coalition; cases involved rape (406) and gang rape (160). cases.title: Lumos — 'Funding Haitian Orphanages at the Cost of Children's Rights'

cases.what: Lumos researched Haiti's orphanages from October 2016 to February 2017, including a 2016 evaluation of 140 children in four orphanages with the government agency IBESR, and published its report in June 2017. It found at least US$70 million a year going to about a third of orphanages, with total funding estimated above $100 million a year; only 15% of orphanages were registered and at least 140 had conditions putting children at severe risk. It documented violence and severe neglect and, in a few cases, sexual abuse, trafficking and avoidable deaths, and evidence of orphanages recruiting children away from families — an 'orphanage business' it describes as increasingly recognised as trafficking.

patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: MONUC peacekeepers — sexual exploitation of girls in Bunia (OIOS 2004)
cases.who: UN Organization Mission in the DRC (MONUC) military contingents, military observers and civilian staff
cases.what: After media and Congolese women's reports in March and May 2004, OIOS investigated in Bunia from May to September 2004. It found that sexual contact with peacekeepers occurred 'with regularity', usually in exchange for food or small sums of money, and that many cases involved girls under 18, some as young as 13. Of 72 allegations reported to MONUC, many could not be investigated because they were non-specific; six cases were fully substantiated. The findings led to the Secretary-General asking Prince Zeid Ra'ad Al-Hussein of Jordan to prepare the 2005 comprehensive report on SEA by peacekeepers.
cases.network: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)

cases.title: DR Congo — UN-verified sexual violence and abduction of children by M23, FARDC and armed groups (2024)
cases.who: M23 (68), CODECO (63), FARDC (47), Raia Mutomboki, Nyatura, ADF and others
cases.what: The UN verified sexual violence against 358 girls in the DRC in 2024, by M23 (68), CODECO (63), the Armed Forces of the DRC (47), Raia Mutomboki (33), Nyatura (24) and others, and the abduction of 815 children, by ADF (265), M23 (178) and others. In 2022 it verified sexual violence against 284 children aged 4 to 17, 56 of them by FARDC.

cases.title: MINUSCA peacekeepers — rapes near Bambari airport
cases.who: MINUSCA contingents believed by survivors to be from the Republic of Congo or DR Congo
cases.what: Human Rights Watch documented eight cases of sexual exploitation and abuse by MINUSCA peacekeepers during research in Bambari in January 2016, including a 14-year-old girl and an 18-year-old woman who said they were gang-raped near Bambari airport. Most incidents occurred between September and December 2015, when a Republic of Congo contingent guarded the airport.
cases.network: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)

cases.title: MINUSCA — DR Congo battalion repatriated after child abuse allegations
cases.who: Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) battalion serving with MINUSCA
cases.what: About 800 troops from the Democratic Republic of the Congo served with the UN mission in the Central African Republic (MINUSCA) in 2015. In August 2015 three Congolese peacekeepers were accused of raping three female civilians, including a minor. In January 2016 MINUSCA confirmed the Congolese unit would withdraw and not be replaced, after a UN review of its equipment, vetting procedures and preparedness; it was not clear whether the abuse allegations were the main factor. The UN's 2016 allegations tables (A/71/818) list 17 allegations involving DRC military personnel in MINUSCA, with 15 child victims.
cases.network: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)

cases.title: DR Congo — forced labour and sexual exploitation of children at eastern artisanal mines (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Mining bosses, miners, family members, government officials, armed groups
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says mining bosses, other miners, family members, government officials and armed groups force or coerce adults and children into forced labour in artisanal mines in eastern DRC, including through debt bondage, and that most trafficking is internal, including sex trafficking and forced marriage of girls.
cases.cover_up: Traffickers named in the report include government officials; corruption and complicity contributed to impunity.

cases.title: Ebola response, North Kivu & Ituri — Independent Commission on SEA by WHO and other responders
cases.who: WHO staff and contractors, Ministry of Health and partner personnel in the 10th Ebola response
cases.what: The Independent Commission appointed by WHO reported on 28 September 2021 that it identified 83 alleged perpetrators, 21 of whom were established with certainty as WHO employees during the response; most were Congolese staff hired temporarily who used their authority to obtain sex, often in exchange for jobs. The review team heard 63 women and 12 men aged 13 to 43; the youngest, a girl selling phone cards in Mangina in April 2019, said a WHO driver raped her. Nine rape allegations were recorded and 29 women and girls became pregnant.

cases.title: Lord's Resistance Army — child abduction and sexual slavery; ICC conviction of Dominic Ongwen
cases.who: Lord's Resistance Army (LRA), leader Joseph Kony (ICC warrant outstanding)
cases.what: The LRA abducted tens of thousands of children in northern Uganda for use as fighters, porters and 'wives'; UNICEF estimated at least 25,000 by 2006. On 4 February 2021 ICC Trial Chamber IX convicted Sinia Brigade commander Dominic Ongwen, himself abducted as a child, of 61 crimes including rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage, forced pregnancy and the conscription and use of children under 15 (2002–2005); he was sentenced to 25 years on 6 May 2021, confirmed on appeal 15 December 2022. From 2008 the LRA abducted thousands more in DR Congo, South Sudan and CAR.

cases.title: Bosco Ntaganda (UPC/FPLC, Ituri) — ICC conviction incl. rape and sexual slavery of child soldiers
cases.who: Union of Congolese Patriots (UPC) / Patriotic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (FPLC)
cases.what: On 8 July 2019 ICC Trial Chamber VI found Bosco Ntaganda guilty of 18 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Ituri in 2002–2003, including rape, sexual slavery and the conscription and use of children under 15; he was the first person convicted of sexual slavery by the ICC. He was sentenced to 30 years on 7 November 2019, confirmed on appeal on 30 March 2021. He had told child soldiers, 'When you're a soldier, you get a woman for free'.

cases.title: Thomas Lubanga (UPC, Ituri) — ICC's first conviction: conscription and use of children
cases.who: Union of Congolese Patriots (UPC/FPLC)
cases.what: On 14 March 2012 the ICC found Thomas Lubanga guilty of enlisting and conscripting children under 15 and using them in hostilities, and sentenced him on 10 July 2012 to 14 years; the verdict was confirmed on 1 December 2014. Sexual violence against girl soldiers was raised at trial but not charged. He was released on 15 March 2020 after serving his sentence.

cases.title: LRA Makombo massacre and abductions, DR Congo (2009)
cases.who: Lord's Resistance Army commanders Lt. Col. Binansio Okumu ('Binany') and 'Obol', reporting to Gen. Dominic Ongwen (per HRW)
cases.what: From 14 to 17 December 2009 Lord's Resistance Army forces attacked at least 10 villages in the remote Makombo area of Haute-Uélé, north-eastern DR Congo, killing at least 321 civilians and abducting 250 others, including at least 80 children. Human Rights Watch, which documented the previously unreported massacre after a field mission in February 2010, said it was carried out by two LRA commanders who reported to Gen. Dominic Ongwen, the senior LRA leader believed to command its forces in Congo and wanted by the International Criminal Court.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: Greece — about 4,000 children adopted abroad 1950–1975; 2025 citizenship law.
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children from their families were carried out by governments as a matter of policy. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, about 500 babies were taken from mothers held in detention and given to other families; in 2012 a court found this had been a "systematic plan", and by July 2025, 140 of those children had been identified. Under Franco's dictatorship in Spain, children were taken from Republican mothers and later from unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children from their families and placed them in residential schools or with non-Indigenous families. In 1951 Denmark sent a group of Greenlandic children to live with Danish families, and France moved children from the island of Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported children from occupied parts of Ukraine; in March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over these deportations.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Greece — about 4,000 children adopted abroad 1950–1975; 2025 citizenship law; Lechaina Children's Care Centre, Greece — caged beds and sedation.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 238 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
cases.who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
cases.what: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.

cases.title: Lechaina Children's Care Centre, Greece — caged beds and sedation
cases.who: State Children Care Center of Lechaina (children with disabilities)
cases.what: In March 2011 the Greek Ombudsman's Office published a report on the state care centre at Lechaina finding too few doctors and nurses, systematic sedation, residents tied to their beds and the use of wooden cage beds because of staff shortages; most children received no education. In 2012 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child expressed deep concern about the centre. A BBC report in 2014 found conditions had barely improved. This is a record of institutional abuse and neglect; no sexual-abuse finding was located.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Greece — about 4,000 children adopted abroad 1950–1975; 2025 citizenship law
cases.who: Greek state institutions and foundling homes; AHEPA and other US agencies and proxy-adoption intermediaries
cases.what: Between 1950 and 1975 as many as 4,000 Greek-born children, many called 'orphans' after the civil war or born 'illegitimate', were adopted in the United States, the Netherlands and Sweden through hastily conducted procedures. A law published on 2 May 2025 recognised their adopted status, restored a path to Greek citizenship and eased access to records. The Greek state promised an investigation in the late 1950s that has not been carried out.
cases.cover_up: The adoptions were covered by confidentiality and secrecy; many adoptees lacked papers proving their origins.

cases.title: 764 network — founder sentenced to 80 years
cases.who: 764 (online network on Discord/Telegram; founder Bradley Cadenhead)
cases.what: 764, named after the first digits of the ZIP code of Stephenville, Texas, extorted minors into producing abuse material, self-harm and animal cruelty. Its founder, Bradley Cadenhead, was arrested in August 2021 aged 16 and on 16 May 2023 was sentenced in Texas to 80 years after pleading guilty to nine counts of possession/promotion of child sexual abuse material. The US DOJ describes 764 as a nihilistic violent extremist network and its Counterterrorism Section prosecutes it; on 29 April 2025 DOJ announced the arrests of two alleged leaders of the subgroup '764 Inferno', in North Carolina and in Greece. On 10 December 2025 Canada became the first country to list 764 as a terrorist entity.

cases.title: Europol: at least 10,000 unaccompanied migrant children missing in Europe (2016)
cases.who: Europol; organized crime exploiting the migrant flow
cases.what: On 31 January 2016 Europol's chief of staff Brian Donald told The Observer that at least 10,000 unaccompanied children had disappeared after arriving in Europe, 5,000 of them in Italy and 1,000 in Sweden, and that Europol had evidence some had been sexually exploited. He said an entire criminal infrastructure had developed over 18 months around exploiting the migrant flow, with many arrests in Germany and Hungary. Save the Children estimated 26,000 unaccompanied children arrived in 2015.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: New Zealand DIA-led operation: 146 children safeguarded
cases.who: Tens of thousands of accounts sharing abuse material on an online service
cases.what: Begun in 2019 after an online service provider reported offenders exchanging imagery of the sadistic abuse of infants and children. By March 2022 it had opened 836 cases internationally, led to 46 arrests across New Zealand, identified more than 100 suspects in the EU and safeguarded 146 children; in Austria and Hungary suspects were abusing their own children.

cases.title: Germany, Spain, Italy, Greece — romance-method pimps, Nigerian networks, unaccompanied children (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: 'Loverboy' traffickers; Nigerian cult-linked groups; Eastern European recruiters
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP reports say young male traffickers in Germany and Spain coerce girls into sex trafficking through sham romantic relationships; highly organized groups sometimes linked to Nigerian cult organizations exploit Nigerian women and girls in Germany and Italy, in Italy through debt and 'voodoo' rituals; Eastern European girls are recruited online for child sex trafficking in Italy; and in Greece unaccompanied children are vulnerable to sex trafficking and Roma children from Albania, Bulgaria and Romania are forced to beg.

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: Denmark — 1951 'little Danes' experiment: 22 Greenlandic children removed
cases.who: Danish government, Danish Red Cross, Save the Children Denmark
cases.what: In May 1951 Danish authorities, with Save the Children Denmark, had teachers and priests in Greenland identify children aged six to ten, and 22 Inuit children were sent to Danish foster families to be re-educated as 'little Danes'; many families were reluctant. About a year and a half later 16 returned to Greenland, where they were placed in a children's home built by the Danish Red Cross and many never lived with their families again; six were adopted in Denmark. A 2020 report found half later had mental health problems. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen apologised in December 2020, and in March 2022, after legal action, the six survivors were each awarded 250,000 kroner.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Operation Hamlet — parents sharing abuse of their own children
cases.who: International online network of offenders, many abusing their own children
cases.what: Danish National Police, acting on information from Save the Children about images found online, arrested a man and his wife who had posted images of the abuse of their nine-year-old daughter; from November 2001 the US Customs CyberSmuggling Center coordinated US inquiries with Danish police, INTERPOL and NCMEC. On 9 August 2002 US Customs announced 10 arrests of US citizens, with 10 more suspects arrested in Denmark, Belgium, Germany, England, Switzerland and the Netherlands, and 45 children rescued, 37 of them in the US; in many cases parents were abusing their own children. Fifteen suspects, five of them foreign nationals, were indicted on federal conspiracy charges in the Eastern District of California on 8 August 2002.

cases.title: Operation Long Arm — 'Bamse' bulletin board (1992)
cases.who: Bamse BBS (Danish bulletin board, ~900 users)
cases.what: US Customs' first major case against internet child abuse material. In late 1992 a US Customs controlled delivery led to a suspect who said he had obtained images from a Europe-based bulletin board; agents found 'Bamse', a Danish bulletin board with child abuse rooms, and two other Danish boards using its images, where users paid a subscription or supplied images of their own. Working with Danish authorities, the operation led to about 35 arrests and convictions in the US. Start year approximate.

cases.title: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
cases.who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
cases.what: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

cases.title: Godhavn Report — Danish state children's homes 1945–1976
cases.who: Danish state-run children's homes incl. Godhavn boys' home
cases.what: The Godhavn Report, published 9 May 2011, examined Godhavn boys' home and 18 other state homes from 1945 to 1976, finding neglect, physical and sexual abuse, and that about 22% of Godhavn residents had been given psychiatric drugs by psychiatrist Ib Ostenfeld. No prosecutions followed. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen apologised to hundreds of victims in 2019.

cases.title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
cases.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

cases.title: Europol sprint on buyers of live-distant abuse in the Philippines (2024)
cases.who: Buyers worldwide directing livestreamed abuse by traffickers in the Philippines
cases.what: From 24 to 28 June 2024, 32 investigators at Europol processed leads from US HSI investigations into networks exploiting children in the Philippines: over 10 million lines of chat between about 12,000 customer accounts and 100 seller accounts, built up over 12 years. The sprint produced information packages that may lead authorities in 24 countries to 197 buyers. Europol notes buyers direct traffickers to abuse children in real time on webcam and some travel to the Philippines to abuse children in person.

patterns.pattern_summary: Armed groups have abducted, enslaved and sold children as a deliberate practice. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, against girls as young as eight. The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.

cases.title: Uganda — European Adoption Consultants bribery scheme; judges sanctioned
cases.who: European Adoption Consultants (Ohio, defunct); Ugandan lawyers and judges
cases.what: Between 2013 and 2016 the Ohio agency European Adoption Consultants arranged the adoption of more than 30 Ugandan children by US families; families were promised their children would attend school in Kampala but they were taken to an unlicensed home. On 14 August 2020 a federal indictment charged two EAC employees and Ugandan lawyer Dorah Mirembe (allegations; presumed innocent); an earlier employee, Robin Longoria, pleaded guilty in August 2019 to bribing Ugandan officials. On 17–18 August 2020 the US State Department sanctioned Ugandan judges Moses Mukiibi and Wilson Musalu Musene and lawyers Mirembe and Patrick Ecobu.
cases.cover_up: Bribes were paid to Ugandan judges and other officials to secure adoption orders.

cases.title: AMISOM bases, Mogadishu — rape and sexual exploitation (HRW 2014)
cases.who: African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) Ugandan and Burundian contingents
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's report of 8 September 2014, based on 50 interviews including 21 survivors, documented 10 incidents of sexual abuse, including rape and sexual assault, and 14 cases of sexual exploitation by African Union (AMISOM) soldiers, mainly Ugandan personnel at and around AMISOM's headquarters and Burundian personnel at their base in Mogadishu. Four rape cases and one sexual assault involved girls under 18; the youngest was a 12-year-old allegedly raped by a Ugandan soldier near Baidoa in May 2013. Many victims had gone to the bases to seek medicine or aid, including a woman seeking medicine for her sick baby, and interpreters facilitated soldiers' access; some women and girls were compelled into sex in exchange for money, food and medicine.

cases.title: Kenya — child sex trafficking in Kilifi/Kwale villas; Karamoja girls to Nairobi (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Family members, taxi drivers, recruiters; foreign and local offenders
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report cites a 2023 NGO study estimating that more than 2,000 children were exploited in child sex trafficking in Kilifi and Kwale counties, increasingly in private villas and vacation homes rather than hotels. It also reports cross-border rings moving women and underage girls from Uganda's Karamoja region to Nairobi, and truck drivers, miners and Lake Victoria fishermen exploiting children.
cases.cover_up: The report notes ongoing concerns of official complicity with no reported action against complicit officials.

cases.title: Uganda — Karamojong children sold at border markets (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers including community 'elders'
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says NGOs estimate the majority of child sex-trafficking victims in Uganda are ethnically Karamojong, especially from Napak district. Traffickers, sometimes community 'elders', force children to meet them at international borders, where markets are organized to sell children into domestic servitude or sex trafficking. Women, girls and boys are exploited in Kampala brothels, bars and homes.

cases.title: 'Hidden in Plain Sight' — Australian Parliament recognises orphanage trafficking as modern slavery
cases.who: Australian volunteers, donors, schools and tour operators supporting overseas orphanages
cases.what: The Joint Standing Committee's report 'Hidden in Plain Sight', released on 6 December 2017 from its inquiry into establishing a Modern Slavery Act, recognised orphanage trafficking as a form of modern slavery to be covered by the Act. A chapter was devoted to orphanage trafficking, orphanage tourism and Australian donations, with evidence from ReThink Orphanages, Lumos, the ChildSafe campaign and others. Australia's Modern Slavery Act followed in 2018; Lumos supported the change.

cases.title: Lord's Resistance Army — child abduction and sexual slavery; ICC conviction of Dominic Ongwen

cases.what: The LRA abducted tens of thousands of children in northern Uganda for use as fighters, porters and 'wives'; UNICEF estimated at least 25,000 by 2006. On 4 February 2021 ICC Trial Chamber IX convicted Sinia Brigade commander Dominic Ongwen, himself abducted as a child, of 61 crimes including rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage, forced pregnancy and the conscription and use of children under 15 (2002–2005); he was sentenced to 25 years on 6 May 2021, confirmed on appeal 15 December 2022. From 2008 the LRA abducted thousands more in DR Congo, South Sudan and CAR.

cases.title: Uganda — over 500 unlicensed children's homes outside state oversight

cases.what: Uganda's Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development says only 185 children's homes are fully licensed (holding 9,486 children) and that more than 500 unlicensed institutions operate without oversight, exposing children to neglect, exploitation and abuse. The ministry's principal probation officer said many children in homes are not orphans, and that some are survivors of trafficking or sexual abuse. The government has closed unregistered homes, including Hope Center Uganda (American board) after a raid that found children in poor conditions.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Czech Republic — Fr František Merta.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. cases.what: Human Rights Watch's report of 8 September 2014, based on 50 interviews including 21 survivors, documented 10 incidents of sexual abuse, including rape and sexual assault, and 14 cases of sexual exploitation by African Union (AMISOM) soldiers, mainly Ugandan personnel at and around AMISOM's headquarters and Burundian personnel at their base in Mogadishu. patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. cases.cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).

cases.what: The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar found in 2018 that hundreds of Rohingya women and girls were raped during the 2017 'clearance operations', 80% of corroborated cases being gang rapes, and its August 2019 report found sexual and gender-based violence a 'hallmark' of Tatmadaw operations in Rakhine, Kachin and Shan. cases.title: Bangladesh — girls trafficked to India, Pakistan and the Gulf; Rohingya girls near Cox's Bazar (US TIP 2025)

cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit Bangladeshi women and girls in sex trafficking abroad, including in India, Pakistan and Gulf countries, and observers estimate children are 40 per cent of Bangladeshi sex-trafficking victims exploited abroad. patterns.pattern_summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. The UN has published yearly counts of these allegations against peacekeepers since 2004.

cases.title: Mamou Alliance Academy — missionary children's boarding school, Guinea

cases.what: Mamou Alliance Academy boarded the children of C&MA missionaries in West Africa. cases.cover_up: Alumni wrote to C&MA headquarters about abuse from the 1980s for about ten years before an inquiry was set up.

cases.title: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
cases.who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
cases.what: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; it held over 250,000 unique videos and its server had more than one million Bitcoin addresses, one per account. IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.
cases.cover_up: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.

cases.what: Durov was arrested at Le Bourget airport on 24 August 2024 and on 28 August a Paris investigating judge placed him under formal investigation on all the charges for which he was arrested, including suspected complicity in running a platform allowing illicit transactions, images of child sexual abuse, drug trafficking and fraud, and refusal to communicate information to authorities. He was released on 5 million euros bail, required to report to police twice a week and barred from leaving France. On 4 December 2024 the IWF announced Telegram would use its hashes of known abuse images to detect such material in public parts of the platform; the IWF said it had confirmed thousands of reports of abuse imagery on Telegram since 2022.

patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases on this map the sources give two dates: the year a complaint first reached the police, a church, an employer or another official body, and the year someone was first charged, convicted or named in an official finding. In 1970 Smith was assured he would not be prosecuted. In 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged. Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958, and he was never charged while he was alive. cases.what: US-born Divine Word missionary Richard Daschbach founded the Topu Honis children's shelter in Oecusse in 1992. After a complaint to his superiors in February 2018 he admitted the abuse to them in March 2018, and the Vatican dismissed him from the priesthood on 6 November 2018; the church did not tell the public. He was arrested in April 2019 and charged with 14 counts of sexually abusing children under 14, plus child abuse material and domestic violence counts. On 21 December 2021 a court in Oecusse sentenced him to 12 years, basing the verdict on the testimony of four victims. A report by the Dili archdiocese's Justice and Peace Commission had defended him.

cases.title: Bishop Carlos Ximenes Belo — Vatican sanctions

cases.what: On 28 September 2022 Dutch magazine De Groene Amsterdammer reported that two men said Bishop Belo had abused them and other boys in Fatumaca and Dili, before and during his time as bishop. The next day the Vatican confirmed it had received allegations in 2019 and imposed disciplinary sanctions in 2020: limits on movement and ministry, no contact with minors and no contact with Timor-Leste. The sanctions were reinforced in 2021. Belo had left Timor in 2002 and worked in Maputo, Mozambique from 2004.
cases.cover_up: Vatican received allegations in 2019 and imposed sanctions in 2020 but did not disclose them until a magazine reported the case in 2022

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children

patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children from their families were carried out by governments as a matter of policy. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, about 500 babies were taken from mothers held in detention and given to other families; in 2012 a court found this had been a "systematic plan", and by July 2025, 140 of those children had been identified. Under Franco's dictatorship in Spain, children were taken from Republican mothers and later from unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children from their families and placed them in residential schools or with non-Indigenous families. In 1951 Denmark sent a group of Greenlandic children to live with Danish families, and France moved children from the island of Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported children from occupied parts of Ukraine; in March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over these deportations.

patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Gulf states block Roblox over child safety (2025)
cases.who: Roblox Corporation
cases.what: In August 2025 Qatar blocked access to Roblox (13 August) and Kuwait's telecoms regulator temporarily blocked it (21 August) after parents and community groups raised child-safety concerns; Turkey had blocked it on 7 August. Roblox had been banned in Oman and Jordan since 2020, and was banned in the UAE from 2018 to 2021. Wikipedia additionally reports that Bahraini MPs drafted a ban, Palestine announced a ban in November 2025, Kazakhstan's and Kyrgyzstan's authorities warned parents about predators, and Buenos Aires and three Argentine provinces blocked it on school devices after grooming reports.

patterns.pattern: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
patterns.role_note: Filed 15-16 Jan 2019 after Guam's 2016 permanent window; claims rose to nearly 280; Jan 2020 plan offered $21m; sold Yona property for $6.1m. Former Archbishop Anthony Apuron found guilty in a canonical trial (2018-19).
patterns.pattern_summary: Most people abused as children do not tell anyone for many years. In many countries and US states the legal deadline for suing or prosecuting, called a statute of limitations, used to run out in a person's early twenties, before most had spoken. When legislatures proposed extending these deadlines or reopening old claims, the institutions that would face lawsuits lobbied against the changes. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million on lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018. In Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Pennsylvania Catholic Conference spent more than $7.6 million and the state's insurance federation nearly $20.7 million on lobbying from 2014 to 2024. These totals cover all the issues they lobbied on, not only this one. Where the deadlines were lifted anyway, many institutions filed for bankruptcy. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and religious orders did so, several of them hours or days before a trial, a deposition or a new law took effect. The Boy Scouts of America and USA Gymnastics also filed.

cases.title: Archdiocese of Agaña — Archbishop Apuron and bankruptcy
cases.who: Archdiocese of Agaña; former Archbishop Anthony Apuron
cases.what: A Vatican tribunal of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith found former Archbishop Anthony Apuron guilty of some charges including sexual abuse of minors in March 2018; the appeal was rejected in February 2019. He was barred from office and from living in Guam but not laicised; he denies the allegations. The archdiocese filed for bankruptcy in January 2019 facing more than 200 lawsuits naming 35 clergy, teachers and scoutmasters. Guam lifted the civil statute of limitations in 2016.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2009: suspension: Kyrgyzstan suspends intercountry adoption (US State Dept adoption alert April 2010)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.
